title: Ex 5.24 · Multiplying congruences
prompt: Let $a, b, c, d, n$ be integers with $n \ge 1$. Prove that if $a \equiv b \pmod n$ and $c \equiv d \pmod n$, then $ac \equiv bd \pmod n$, that is, $n \mid (ac - bd)$.
answer_format: A structured proof: let, case, expr and witness steps (notes optional). No final answer box.
hints: Write a = nj + b and c = nk + d, with two different new letters.
Multiply them out; the bd terms cancel and n divides everything else.
solution: Since $n \mid (a - b)$ and $n \mid (c - d)$: $a = nj + b$ and $c = nk + d$ for integers $j, k$.
$ac - bd = (nj + b)(nk + d) - bd = n^2jk + njd + nkb = n(njk + jd + kb)$.
The bracket is an integer, so $n \mid (ac - bd)$. $\blacksquare$

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses Definition 5.1 (congruence).

steps.content: n^2 j k + n j d + n k b
n j k + j d + k b
